content: Individuals who are known to be HIV-positive should refer to the guidelines for intensified tuberculosis (TB) case-finding and isoniazid preventive therapy in resource-limited settings. These guidelines include specific algorithms (2a–d) that involve interviews about TB symptoms and HIV status. If a person exhibits any of the following symptoms—cough of any duration, hemoptysis, weight loss, fever, or night sweats—further investigation for TB is warranted. Chest radiography should be considered as a secondary screening tool for individuals who screen positive based on symptom assessment. If the chest radiograph shows abnormalities suggestive of TB, the individual should undergo further evaluation for TB. Another set of algorithms (3a–b) incorporates both chest radiography and interviews about HIV status. Individuals with abnormal chest radiographs indicative of TB should also be evaluated further. Each algorithm for adults includes options for initial diagnostic testing for those who screen positive, such as sputum-smear microscopy or rapid molecular tests like the Xpert MTB/RIF assay. These tests have demonstrated high accuracy for both smear-positive and smear-negative pulmonary TB. Positive or negative diagnostic results may necessitate repeat testing or additional diagnostic evaluations, including culture, drug-susceptibility testing, clinical assessment, or a combination of these methods. Culture remains the gold standard for TB diagnosis but is not recommended as an initial diagnostic test in these algorithms due to its resource-intensive nature and longer turnaround time (2–6 weeks) compared to Xpert MTB/RIF or sputum-smear microscopy, which provide results in less than a day. In settings where resources allow, chest radiographs suggestive of TB can be categorized into those indicative of active TB and those suggestive of either active or inactive TB. Conventional light microscopy, using Ziehl–Neelsen staining or fluorescence microscopy (including LED-based microscopy), is commonly employed for examining direct smears. However, the health system must have sufficient capacity to ensure follow-up after culture results become available. In such cases, culture may be used alongside or after testing with Xpert MTB/RIF or sputum-smear microscopy. Drug-susceptibility testing should follow the guidelines for diagnosing drug-resistant TB. The choice of algorithm depends on the risk group being assessed, the prevalence of TB, resource availability, and feasibility. In populations with moderate or low TB prevalence, it is crucial to use algorithms with high specificity to avoid a low positive predictive value and reduce the proportion of false-positive TB cases. For example, when TB prevalence is 5% in the screened population, all algorithms have a positive predictive value of less than 75% when clinical diagnosis (using chest radiography and clinical evaluation) is applied to individuals with negative initial diagnostic test results. Even without clinical diagnosis, the positive predictive value is below 80% for all but one algorithm (algorithm 1d: screening for cough lasting longer than 2 weeks, followed by chest radiography and Xpert MTB/RIF testing). Ensuring high-quality diagnostic procedures and clinical assessments is essential, particularly in settings with moderate to low TB prevalence. If the positive predictive value is low, repeat tests or confirmatory culture may be necessary. When TB prevalence is 1% or higher, the positive predictive value exceeds 80% for some algorithms (1b–d, 2d, and 3b, excluding clinical diagnosis). However, diagnostic quality must still be optimized. In high-risk groups where the consequences of missed or delayed diagnosis and treatment are severe, algorithms with very high sensitivity should be used, even if this results in lower specificity. The risk of false-positive diagnoses of active TB must also be considered in these groups. However, the benefits of early treatment may outweigh the risks of treating a false-positive case. For individuals eligible for latent TB infection treatment (e.g., contacts younger than 5 years and people living with HIV), ruling out active TB is more critical than avoiding a false-positive diagnosis. Sensitivity is therefore prioritized over specificity for such individuals. In many settings, high-quality chest radiography and trained personnel to interpret the images may not be available. Similarly, the Xpert MTB/RIF test may not be accessible in all settings. In such cases, the priority should be to integrate these tests into routine diagnostic services before considering their use in screening programs. Individuals known or suspected to have TB and at high risk of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) should always undergo Xpert MTB/RIF testing as the primary diagnostic test if available. This group includes individuals suspected of pulmonary TB who are at risk of harboring MDR-TB bacilli, as defined by national policies or WHO guidelines. These groups include individuals previously treated with anti-TB medicines and diagnosed again with pulmonary TB (e.g., retreatment categories such as failure, default, or relapse). When the prevalence of rifampicin resistance in the screened population is less than 10%, a positive Xpert MTB/RIF result for rifampicin resistance should be confirmed with conventional drug-susceptibility testing or line probe assays. All algorithms include an interview about HIV status. Offering HIV counseling and testing should be an integral part of TB screening, especially in settings with high HIV prevalence, to improve the performance of the screening algorithm and facilitate early diagnosis, treatment, and care for people with HIV. Children aged 10 years and older should be screened using the same algorithm as adults. No published studies have specifically assessed the sensitivity and specificity of screening algorithms for children and adolescents who are not contacts of TB patients. However, the Guideline Development Group believes that the adult screening algorithm is likely to have similar accuracy in children aged 10 years and older. For algorithm 1, screening for cough lasting longer than 2 weeks has low sensitivity. The overall sensitivity of the algorithm is further reduced when sputum-smear microscopy is used for diagnosis. The sensitivity of sputum-smear microscopy varies depending on the quality of smear preparation and reading, as well as the proportion of smear-positive TB cases among culture-positive cases in the tested population. Sensitivity can be improved with various sputum-processing methods and fluorescence microscopy, but these methods may reduce specificity. The specificity of sputum-smear microscopy depends on factors such as the case definition, the prevalence of nontuberculous mycobacteria, the gold standard used for assessment, and the quality of slide preparation and reading. Using WHO’s case definition of identifying one positive smear out of two, the pooled specificity for conventional smear microscopy is 98% (95% confidence interval: 93–99%), but it may be lower when different methods are used to improve sensitivity. A 1% reduction in specificity from 99% to 98% doubles the number of false-positive cases when the prevalence in the screened group is low. False-positive diagnoses caused by inappropriate smear preparation or reading, contamination, or operational errors can be reduced by repeating tests for those who test positive or by performing alternative confirmatory diagnostic tests. Therefore, additional testing should be considered when TB prevalence is low. Because sputum-smear microscopy has low sensitivity, additional diagnostic evaluation is often required for individuals with negative test results, especially in high TB prevalence settings where the negative predictive value is reduced. The specificity of diagnosing smear-negative TB based on chest radiography and clinical evaluation is low (approximately 94%), leading to a high number of false-positive cases if a large proportion of individuals with negative sputum-smear microscopy undergo clinical diagnosis. At a TB prevalence of up to 2% in the screened population, the positive predictive value for all algorithms is less than 75% when sputum-smear microscopy is used as the initial diagnostic test and clinical diagnosis is considered for those who test negative by sputum-smear microscopy. It is therefore critical to optimize the accuracy of sputum-smear microscopy and clinical diagnosis, particularly when the prevalence in the screened population is less than 2%. If high-quality culture is available, it can be used to improve the specificity of the final diagnosis. The Xpert MTB/RIF test has higher sensitivity than sputum-smear microscopy, but the overall sensitivity of the algorithm is limited by the low sensitivity of screening for cough lasting longer than 2 weeks. Repeat testing with Xpert MTB/RIF or further diagnostic evaluation and testing with culture may be required for individuals with a high clinical suspicion of TB. Using Xpert MTB/RIF as a follow-up test for individuals with negative sputum-smear microscopy improves both the sensitivity and specificity of diagnosing smear-negative TB compared to clinical diagnosis. If Xpert MTB/RIF is available at the point of care (or sputum transportation can be organized for everyone tested), it should ideally be used as the initial test instead of sputum-smear microscopy. At a 1% prevalence of TB in the screened population, 94% of individuals who screen positive will test negative by sputum-smear microscopy. Therefore, the number of Xpert MTB/RIF tests will be reduced only marginally by using sputum-smear microscopy first, and 94% of those who screen positive but are smear-negative will be tested by both sputum-smear microscopy and Xpert MTB/RIF. Moreover, the total number of false-positive cases will be higher if sputum-smear microscopy is used first. When Xpert MTB/RIF is available only through referral (e.g., to tertiary-level facilities), it can be used as part of further diagnostic evaluation for individuals who are sputum smear-negative and have a high likelihood of TB. The specificity of the Xpert MTB/RIF test is high (99%). However, at a 5% prevalence, the positive predictive value is only 75%. Repeat testing and further diagnostic evaluation can reduce the number of false-positive cases. Using chest radiography as a second screening test after positive symptom screening significantly improves specificity and reduces sensitivity only marginally. A second screen with chest radiography followed by sputum-smear microscopy yields not only a high proportion of false-negative cases but also a high proportion of false-positive cases. Furthermore, individuals with both a cough lasting longer than 2 weeks and an abnormal chest radiograph suggestive of TB but who are sputum smear-negative usually require further clinical evaluation since the negative predictive value is low. This further reduces overall specificity and generates additional false-positive cases. Therefore, screening with chest radiography should ideally be followed by testing with Xpert MTB/RIF, which has higher negative and positive predictive values than sputum-smear microscopy. Using chest radiography as a second screening test reduces the number of Xpert MTB/RIF tests required for those who screen positive compared to using only cough lasting longer than 2 weeks. For example, at 1% prevalence, the number of required Xpert MTB/RIF tests per true case is 9 when chest radiography is used as the second screening test, compared to 17 Xpert MTB/RIF tests when chest radiography is not used. Screening with chest radiography may be done for abnormalities suggestive of active TB or for abnormalities suggestive of either active or inactive TB. Algorithm 2 has higher overall sensitivity than Algorithm 1 (71% compared to 32% when Xpert MTB/RIF testing is used for diagnosis). However, it generates a larger number of individuals with positive screening results and therefore requires more resources than Algorithm 1. Algorithm 2 has lower specificity than Algorithm 1. At 1% prevalence, the positive predictive value for a positive Xpert MTB/RIF test is 69%, and it is only 40% for positive sputum-smear microscopy, whereas Algorithm 1 has positive predictive values of 85% for a positive Xpert MTB/RIF and 67% for a positive sputum smear. Algorithm 2 should be used for risk groups where high sensitivity is important and for whom the negative consequences of a false-positive diagnosis are less severe. When high sensitivity is required, the Xpert MTB/RIF test is the preferred diagnostic test. The same principles for improving the specificity of the final diagnosis as described for Algorithm 1 apply to Algorithm 2. Similar to Algorithm 1, using chest radiography for the second screening in Algorithm 2 significantly improves the specificity and positive predictive value of the final diagnosis. It also reduces the number of Xpert MTB/RIF tests required while reducing sensitivity only marginally. Screening with chest radiography may be done for abnormalities suggestive of active TB or for abnormalities suggestive of either active or inactive TB.
